Tony Zappia I have listened to all of the opposition speakers who have spoken on the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 and all I heard from each and every one of them was an attack on the unions, an attack on the minister, talk about refugee policy, which has nothing to do with this bill whatsoever, and talk about border protection. Not once did any member opposite specifically address the substance and the merits of this bill, which seeks to ensure that Australia's interests in offshore projects are indeed protected. I commend the member for Wills, who pointed that out so well and so clearly in his contribution to this debate. Coalition members would like to see the multinationals that control the resource industry in Australia, both onshore and offshore, continue to operate without any restrictions and responsibilities. It is time that that came to an end. There is no logical reason whatsoever why the resources that are found offshore should be treated differently to the resources found on land in Australia and why workers who work on those resources on land should be treated any differently to the workers who are dealing with the resources found in the oceans. This legislation arises from the Federal Court decision in the Allseas v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship case. The court found that the foreign workers in that case—those on board the two pipe-laying vessels _Lorelay_ and _Solitaire_were not within the Australian migration zone and therefore did not require Australian visas. As a result of that decision, a task force was convened. I make it clear that that was done by the previous minister for immigration, not the current minister, whom members opposite seek to condemn and criticise because of what they refer to as his self-interest in this matter. The task force was asked to consider a response to the Federal Court decision so as to ensure that those projects did in fact fall within Australian jurisdiction. I note that th

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2013-06-27.66.1) to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5086) main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that the Senate can now discuss it in more detail. ### What was the bill's main idea? The [bill was introduced](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5086) *"to provide that foreign workers who participate in, or support, offshore resources activities are taken to be in the migration zone and are required to hold a visa."* Read more about the bill and its background in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd010).
John Hogg The question now is that the remaining stages of this bill be agreed to and this bill be now passed.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, arguing it is designed to appease the Maritime Union of Australia, which has donated $3 million to Labor since the 2010 election, and to overturn a May 2012 Federal Court ruling in the Allseas case that offshore pipeline workers did not need visas, and announced the coalition would seek to refer the bill to a Senate committee.

Argued for the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, responding to the Federal Court's Allseas ruling that offshore pipeline workers were outside the migration zone, and noted up to 200 vessels service the offshore oil and gas industry, over two-thirds of them foreign-flagged, with the bill expected to commence in early 2014.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, calling it a union power grab that could cost employers up to $30,000 per union right-of-entry visit to offshore rigs, questioned its border security value given 44,219 unauthorised arrivals on 723 boats since 2007, and noted only 13 complaints arose from 99 inspections of 156 facilities in 2012.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, warning it threatens a resources pipeline worth more than $100 billion including the $30 billion Olympic Dam project, questioned its border security implications given more than 43,000 unauthorised arrivals under Labor, and accused the government of doing the bidding of unions, which represent only 13 per cent of the private sector workforce.

Argued for the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, defending it as protecting Australian jobs and fair work conditions for offshore workers rather than restricting foreign labour, noting skilled migration already accounts for about two-thirds of Australia's migrant intake, and pointed to past cases of worker abuse on foreign-flagged vessels in Australian waters.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 as a fix for the Allseas Federal Court decision that let offshore workers escape Australian labour law, but flagged a technical loophole covering vessels like dredgers that the Greens will push to close in the Senate.

Summing up debate on the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, argued the offshore migration provisions dating to 1982, before the exclusive economic zone existed, must be updated after the Federal Court's May 2012 Allseas decision, and announced consultation on a new visa pathway before the new requirement takes effect next year.

The speaker argued the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 was drafted by former Prime Minister Gillard and Minister O'Connor to benefit the Maritime Union of Australia, not the national interest, and that it would drive international vessels and expertise away from Australian waters. The speaker also claimed the bill was introduced without proper consultation, a regulation impact statement, or consideration of Australia's international law of the sea obligations.

Sophie Mirabella I rise to speak on the so-called Australian Jobs Bill 2013. In doing so I wish to express my frustration with not only the content of the bill but the government's lack of accountability in explaining and justifying the reasons for its introduction and its apparent determination to yet again push through legislation that will increase regulatory and compliance costs for Australian businesses. Given that it has misled the Australian people hundreds and hundreds of times, it is difficult to take almost anything that this government says at face value. But it is even harder to find reason to support one of its bills when there is so little clarification around even the very basic details in the legislation—the precise reasons for the change and exactly how those changes will be financed. Prior to February this year, I cannot recall in my time as a shadow minister ever having been refused a briefing by the government. In February was when my office asked Minister Combet's office if I could receive a briefing from the government following the release of the so-called Industry Innovation Statement—otherwise described as a 'jobs plan', another Orwellian phrase—of which these changes form a part. That request was pointedly refused. One of a number of reasons why I sought that briefing was to try and obtain more detail about the changes to which this bill potentially would give effect. Such conduct points not only to a disturbing lack of accountability on the part of the minister but also to a complete arrogant disregard for accepted protocol, good governance and accountability—especially when a staff member in the minister's office tells a staff member in mine that the basic reason for the refusal is that I apparently had the temerity, the gall, the nerve, to make some public criticisms of a number of elements of the government's policies in this area. Richard Colbeck Prior to question time I was making some comments in relation to the Australian Jobs Bill 2013. In my comments I did not say that the opposition are opposing this piece of legislation, but I did put on the record some of the reasons why we might be doing that. One reason in particular is that this legislation imposes additional costs on industry and on business, which, as I said earlier, is a hallmark of this government. I talked about the fact that this government has imposed the carbon tax on Australian business. The government claims that it has only a small impact, but it does its calculations on an economy-wide basis—it ignores sectoral specifics of the cost of a carbon tax on industry. I know one business, for example, that has spent $17 million to mitigate the cost of the carbon tax on its business. It did receive some government assistance to put a co-generation plant in as a part of that project. That will reduce their energy costs, but not in a net sense. After they have spent that $17 million, after they have received $4 million in taxpayers' assistance to spend that money, they will still have a $7 million a year bill over and above what they had before the carbon tax came in. The government talks about its food and foundries program. Government members were in Wynyard in Tasmania with a company recently, talking about the fact that that company was going to save $140,000 a year on its energy bills, but they did not say what the net cost to the company of the energy bills was. As I said, one business spent $17 million to reduce its energy costs, which it has done, but in a net sense it is still $7 million a year worse off. Criticised the Australian Jobs Bill 2013, revealing her office was refused a ministerial briefing in February after publicly criticising the government's Industry Innovation Statement, disputed the government's claim of a $1 billion research and development funding cut as unverified, and cited more than 140,000 net manufacturing job losses under this government, one every 19 minutes, against 6,000 to 7,000 lost over 11½ years under the Howard government.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill 2013, requiring Australian Industry Participation Plans for projects worth $500 million or more, estimating it could generate up to $6.4 billion in economic activity, and detailed a $24.4 million investment to nearly double antidumping investigators and 10 new industry innovation precincts, while warning a coalition government would cut $500 million from the New Car Plan, with a further $1.5 billion cut planned, threatening 200,000 auto sector jobs.

Rejected the government's approach, saying the coalition would immediately repeal the carbon tax and dismissing the Australian Jobs Bill's title as another example of the government's Orwellian naming of legislation that will not actually create jobs.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill as part of a $1 billion package launched on 17 February, citing modelling showing it could generate $1.6 billion to $6.4 billion in additional work for Australian firms, and highlighted the Tonsley Park redevelopment in her Kingston electorate following Mitsubishi's 2008 closure, noting one in 10 of the nation's manufacturing workers live in her electorate.

Opposed the bill, citing ABS figures showing 682,900 Australians unemployed as of April 2013, an increase of 211,000 or 45 per cent since the government took office, against population growth of 1,858,000, and noted the Treasurer's promised 500,000 new jobs this financial year has delivered only 123,000, while warning the carbon tax will extend to trucking diesel from 1 July 2014, adding 7 cents a litre.

Supported the Australian Jobs Bill, noting manufacturing makes up about 8.3 per cent of employment and 8.6 per cent of GDP yet contributes more than 25 per cent of business R&D investment, cited Australian Steel Institute estimates that local steel wins only 10 to 12 per cent of major resource project work, and credited the $300 million Steel Transformation Plan with keeping BlueScope open.

Opposed the Australian Jobs Bill, noting the existing Australian Industry Participation scheme, introduced by the Howard government in 2001, currently applies to Commonwealth procurements worth $20 million or more, and criticised the government for cutting $25 million from Export Market Development Grants while accumulating $192 billion in debt and offsetting $98.2 million in new spending with an uncosted $1 billion research and development cut.

Summed up the debate on the Australian Jobs Bill, confirming any domestic project worth $500 million or more must produce an Australian Industry Participation Plan, and said Senate committee consultations showed strong stakeholder support for the new Australian Industry Participation Authority established to administer the scheme.

Agreed with the previous speaker's criticism but attributed the destruction of manufacturing instead to the Treasurer letting the dollar rise from 52c to 90c, which he said halved the income of every manufacturer.

The Australian Jobs Bill 2013 was opposed as unlikely to create jobs, with the government's carbon tax, mining tax, and increased costs blamed for job losses in the steel, car, and food-processing industries.

The Australian Jobs Bill 2013 was debated, with opposition senators arguing it imposes additional costs and bureaucracy on business and cuts $1.1 billion from R&D, while crossbench senators Xenophon and Madigan supported lowering the major project threshold from $500 million to $20 million and adding anti-dumping requirements; the bill passed a second reading after the Greens withdrew their amendments.

The amendment removes those sections from the bill which would enable the yes-no case to be sent to households— Honourable Members Honourable members interjecting— Anna Burke Order! As I said in my second reading speech, we believe that it is imperative that the concept of an elector is fundamental to the proper carrying out of an election and, indeed, of a referendum. So we believe that it is vitally important that this provision be removed so that we may return to the situation of the 1984 act, whereby every elector would receive the yes-no case. It would also prevent the Electoral Commissioner from making decisions about which address he may deem the fit one to send material to. As I pointed out in my second reading speech, with regard to emails, there is no available email register. There is no proper knowledge of which people have email addresses and which do not. At this stage, for 2013—it may be different in the future—we should maintain the position of posting, not sending, the yes-no case to every elector as an individual. Lin Thorp As an educationalist, I find it disturbing that this place is being used to consider quite a retrograde step in educational history. There is a movement in education that has been going on since the late eighties, with a move from prescriptive assessment to descriptive assessment, and from time based learning to competency based learning. It is recognising what learning is. It is recognising that individuals learn at different paces and in different methods to come to the same place, which is a level of competency in a particular area. Time based learning is going back to the past. Time based learning presumes that you have a group of students—whether they be young school students or people who are studying, in this case, to be engineers—who are all in the same room, at the same time, with the same teacher, and, at the end of that particular period of time, they are all qualified to do a particular task. That is not the way education works today. Education works today on the acquiring of skills. It does not matter whether it be about learning how to be a barista or how to be a neurosurgeon. I, for one, would prefer, if I were to be under the knife in a serious operation, to know that that particular individual had not just served time at university for a number of years but had reached the level of competency that they deserve. This is what this is all about. Going along with the analogy of medical training, in a different job I worked for the medical school of Tasmania. My task was to review the curriculum of the six-year course for all students doing a Bachelor of Medicine and a Bachelor of Medical Science. What became very clear during that exercise was that so much of that training was time based and it needed to move. Over the years, more and more had been added to the curriculum, based simply on facts and figures, rote learning, if you like, and it needed in to be brought up to the end of the 20th century, as it was then—this was back in the 1990s. Introduced the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013 to restore maritime safety training standards weakened by the 2012 national shipping law, opposing a proposal to cut the required training period for engineer watchkeepers from 36 months to just 12 months.

Introduced the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill to reverse a reduction in training standards caused by the Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law, noting a 2009 agreement between engineers and the safety regulator to enhance qualifications has stalled, and proposed codifying minimum training time after learning the regulator wanted to cut onboard training by two-thirds.

Addressed the bill, explaining concern stems from international changes to seafarer training standards that reduced the minimum requirement from three years to 12 months, reportedly instigated by Iran, and noted the Australian Maritime Safety Authority gave sworn evidence to a Senate estimates hearing on 23 May 2012 that it had no intention of adopting the reduced standard.

Addressed the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill, noting the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers represents around 3,000 marine engineers who raised concerns that a proposed review of Marine Orders Part 3 would water down qualification standards, and said the regulator has since withdrawn its draft order for further consultation, with only four weeks of parliamentary sittings remaining before the election.

Argued that the minority parliament had delivered measures including $13 billion for clean and renewable energy, a tax-free threshold of $18,200, dental treatment from 1 January 2014, and stronger firefighter protections. Supported the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013, defending minimum standards and calling for protections for marine engineers and a safe Australian-owned shipping industry.

Summed up the dispute behind the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill, centred on a proposal to cut required training from three years to one and abolish a mandatory verbal competency test, noting the union had agreed in principle to some reforms while the minister warned the bill would leave Australia with outdated standards inconsistent with global shipping conventions, before the debate was interrupted.

Raised concerns about the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill on National TAFE Day, warning proposed changes could cut required marine engineer training from three years to one year, and urged the minister and the Australian Maritime Safety Authority to renegotiate with the Australian Institute of Marine Engineers to protect shipping safety standards.

Supported the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013, arguing it would prevent Australian marine and power engineering standards from being reduced to lower international standards and would protect vessel, environmental, crew and national security interests.
